background.definition: Paget's disease of bone (osteitis deformans) is a focal skeletal disorder characterized by accelerated bone remodeling that may lead to pain, deformity, or fracture.

list.listitem: Among British women, 0.03/1000 persons/y at age 55 to 59 years; rises to 0.54/1000 persons/y by age 85 years.
Among British men, 0.05 persons/y at age 55 to 59 years; rises to 0.76 persons/y by age 85 years.
More common in populations of Western European ancestry including Great Britain, Western Europe, North America, Australia, and New Zealand.
Uncommon in Scandinavia, southern Europe, Africa, and Asia.
Prevalence in Great Britain and the United States is approximately 2% of the population older than 55 years of age.
An estimated 5% of patients will have symptoms.
It has been estimated that outpatient healthcare costs are approximately 50% higher in patients with Paget's disease compared with matched controls.
Second most common metabolic bone disease (after osteoporosis).
Hypotheses include genetic and/or viral etiologies.
15% to 40% of patients have a first-degree relative with the disease.
Initially, there is an increase in osteoclast activity and number, leading to increased bone resorption. This is followed by increased osteoblast activity, leading to increased bone formation.
The resultant bone tissue is disorganized and of poor structural quality, and the poor-quality bone is susceptible to bowing or fracture.
Adjacent bone marrow is in filtrated by connective tissue and becomes hypervascular. Over time, the accelerated remodeling slows, leaving sclerotic bone.
The process can involve one bone (monostotic) or several bones (polyostotic).
Obtain plain radiographs for at least one site to document the diagnosis.C

Serum alkaline phosphatase is sufficiently sensitive for biochemical diagnosis in most patients, but bone-specific alkaline phosphatase may be needed in patients with low disease activity or concomitant liver disease.C
Urinary markers of bone resorption may also provide an indicator of disease activity but are not usually necessary.C
Obtain a bone scan to document the extent of disease.C
Typical areas of involvement include the skull, vertebrae, pelvis, femur, and tibia.
Most patients are asymptomatic, but bone pain that persists at rest and at night can occur.
A referral populationof 88 patients found that the most common presenting features were bone pain (74%), deformity (18%), deafness (8%) and pathological fracture (6%).
Findings on physical examination can include skeletal deformity, such as bowing of the long bones, and increased skin temperature over involved areas.
Complications can arise depending on the area of involvement and severity (see ).

Diagnostic testing includes biochemical and radiologic studies. Guidelines from US and European endocrine societies recommend plain radiographs if Paget's is suspected, followed by radionuclide bone scan (bone scintigraphy) to determine the extent of disease. The guidelines recommends measurement of serum total alkaline phosphatase or other more specific markers such as P1NP.

Biochemical markers of bone formation include total serum alkaline phosphatase and bone-specific alkaline phosphatase. The sensitivity of bone-specific alkaline phosphatase is approximately 84%, and the sensitivity of total alkaline phosphatase is approximately 78%. Total serum alkaline phosphatase is usually sufficient as a biochemical diagnostic test, but bone-specific alkaline phosphatase can be used in patients with concomitant liver disease, or in those with single-bone involvement in whom total alkaline phosphatase levels may be normal.

Markers of bone resorption include urinary hydroxy proline and urinary N-telopeptide of type I collagen. There are no data showing that markers of bone resorption add diagnostic value, but urine N-telopeptide may be useful in monitoring treatment.

Plain radiographs are only about 67% as sensitive as bone scintigraphy (radionuclide bone scan) in detecting areas of involvement but are felt to be more specific. Obtain plain radiographs of at least one skeletal site to establish the diagnosis, as well as a bone scan to document the extent of involvement. Also obtain radiographs of any painful areas to rule out additional causes.
Bone biopsy can be performed but is rarely needed except when malignancy is suspected from radiographic studies.
Paget's disease is often incidentally discovered radiographically or when serum alkaline phosphatase levels are noted to be high. Occasionally patients present with unexplained bone pain.
History and physical should focus on identifying signs and symptoms that may be related to Paget's disease.
The diagnosis can be made when elevated biochemical markers of bone turnover are found in conjunction with radiographic evidence of Paget's disease.
UK guidelines recommend radionuclide bone scans in addition to radiographs to fully evaluate the extent of metabolically active disease.
The clinical indication with the strongest evidence for the presence of Paget's disease is bone pain. B
Other indications include bone deformity, nerve compression, and involvement of sites thought to be at high risk for complications. C
Bisphosphonates are the first-line medical therapy and have been shown to improve bone pain in symptomatic Paget's disease, with some guidelines recommending zoledronic acid as the preferred agent.A
Subcutaneous calcitonin is an older, now second-line treatment. C

Indications for pharmacologic treatment can be found in . The clinical indication with the strongest evidence for presence of the disease is bone pain; evidence of disease presence for other indications is limited.

Bisphosphonates are the most commonly used agents for medical treatment of Paget's disease. A Cochrane review found good evidence of benefit in terms of pain reduction for bisphosphonates overall. FDA-approved bisphosphonate regimens for Paget's disease can be found in .

The bisphosphonate zoledronic acid may be associated with even higher (and faster) response rates and may be useful in patients who do not respond to or are intolerant of oral bisphosphonates. The 2014 guidelines from the Endocrine Society recommend zoledronic acid 5 mg infused over `5 minutes as the best treatment, as it does not have to be repeated for 5 years in most patients. However, a Cochrane review found higher rates of transient fever or fatigue. Alternatives recommended by this guideline include alendronate 40 mg/day for 6 months, and risedronate 30 mg/day for 2 months. Retreatment with these drugs is typically required within 2 to 5 years.
Use of the potent oral bisphosphonates risedronate and alendronate is associated with normalization of alkaline phosphatase in approximately 55% to 75% of patients, as well as improvement in pain.

A post-marketing surveillance study found that about 70% of patients taking risedronate had normalized their alkaline phosphatase levels. The rate of pain relief was similar for the initial treatment cycle. Common adverse drug reactions included gastrointestinal problems (11%) and hypocalcemia (3.3%).

However, a RCT of intensive vs. symptomatic bisphosphonate therapy in management of Paget’s bone disease concluded that striving to maintain normal ALP levels with intensive bisphosphonate therapy (mostly zoledronic acid) conferred no clinical advantage over symptom-driven management with similar rates of clinical fractures (7.0% vs. 7.4%, respectively) and need for orthopaedic surgery (7.3% vs. 8.3%, respectively). A long term follow-up confirmed these findings, with a trend toward more fractures and orthopedic events in the intensive therapy group.

UK guidelines recommend treatment aimed at improving symptoms rather than treating to achieve a biochemical target. They also recommend zoledronic acid as the bisphosphonate most likely to successfully achieve a reduction in pain.

An observational study found that acute phase reactions following infusion of an aminobisphosphonate are more common in patients with vitamin D deficiency, and suggest that normalizing vitamin D levels prior to the infusion can prevent this.

A study identified 222 persons at risk for Paget's based on genetic markers and randomized them to zoledronic acid or placebo. At the end of the 84 month (7 year) study there was some evidence of better outcomes with active treatment (fewer new or worsening bone lesions).
Calcitonin (given subcutaneously) is an older agent that is rarely used now but can be considered in patients unable to take bisphosphonates.
Analgesic medications (acetaminophen, NSAIDs) may be useful in treatment of minor pain.

Surgery is occasionally needed for management of complications. Fixation of fractures may be needed, and osteotomy may be used for correction of deformity. It is considered second-line to medical therapy and treatment with bisphosphonates should precede surgery according to 2014 US and European guidelines.
Arthroplasty can be used for arthritis not responsive to medical management.
Surgery is occasionally required when symptoms of nerve compression do not respond to medical therapy.

For patients undergoing spinal decompression for lumbar stenosis caused by Paget's disease of bone, adding lumbar fusion is not recommended. Overall complications rates are high in spinal surgery (4 of 15 in one series of published cases).
Walking aids such as shoe lifts, orthotics, or canes may help some patients.
Physical therapy may help improve mobility and functional status.
Instruct patients to avoid immobilization, as it may increase the risk for hypercalcemia.
Hearing loss: use a potent bisphosphonate to prevent hearing loss.
Paralysis: immediate use of a potent IV bisphosphonate, and urgent neurosurgical consultation.
Osteoarthritis: analgesia, and bisphosphonate therapy prior to joint replacement.
Osteosarcoma: consult an orthopedic surgeon, and treat with a bisphosphonate prior to any surgery to reduce bleeding from affected bone.
Biochemical response to bisphosphonate treatment usually occurs within 6 months and lasts for 1 to 2 years. B
Serum alkaline phosphatase testing is adequate in most patients for follow-up. C
Response to treatment may last for several years, but occasionally retreatment is required for symptomatic or biochemical relapse. B
In untreated patients, osteolysis progresses in the long bones at an average rate of 1 cm/y.
Bone pain tends to develop late in the course of the disease, although most patients remain asymptomatic.
Overtime, accelerated bone turnover may subside, leaving areas of sclerotic bone.
Such areas may not appear on bone scans.
Biochemical response to treatment typically lasts for at least 1 year and may last for 2 years or longer.
Some data suggest that retreatment with a more potent bisphosphonate may work in patients who do not respond to initial treatment by 6 months.
In patients who respond to initial treatment, indications for retreatment include relapse of symptoms or an increase in alkaline phosphatase of more than 25% from the nadir.
The most important outcome to monitor is improvement in bone pain.
A systematic review concluded that procollagen type 1 amino-terminal propeptide (P1NP) is the best biomarker for monitoring disease activity, correlating best with the results of scintigraphy.

Biochemical markers can also be followed to assess for efficacy of treatment. Alkaline phosphatase levels may respond at 3 months, typically show a nadir at 6 months, and can be monitored every 6 months thereafter. A reduction of 25% represents a significant response to treatment.
Urinary markers of bone resorption such as N-telopeptide and hydroxy proline may show a response within 1 month of treatment, but such monitoring is usually not clinically necessary.
Routine monitoring of radiographs or bone scans is not necessary.
Sarcomatous transformation of Paget’s disease is a rare complication with a decreasing incidence, male predominance, and poor prognosis.
